etymology: From the Latin costa, a rib or side, through the Old French coste. In the Authorized Version coast means a border or territory generally — the side or edge of a region — and only sometimes a seashore. The modern restriction to the shoreline is a later narrowing.
biblical_def: Coast in the Authorized Version rarely means what a modern reader assumes. It renders the Hebrew gebul, a boundary or territory, and means the border or region of a place whether or not any sea is near it. So the LORD threatens to bring locusts “into thy coast” (Exo 10:4) — into Egypt’s territory, not onto its beaches; Israel passes “by the coast of the land of Edom” (Num 20:23), inland desert country; and Herod, deceived by the wise men, slew all the children “in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof” (Mat 2:16) — Bethlehem being some fifteen miles from the nearest water. The one thing the word insists upon is a boundary, and that is a theme running through the whole Bible. God set the bounds of the nations, appointed the times before appointed and the bounds of their habitation, said to the sea hitherto shalt thou come, but no further, and forbade Israel to remove the ancient landmark which their fathers had set. Occasionally the seashore sense does apply, as when our Lord left Nazareth and dwelt in Capernaum, “which is upon the sea coast” (Mat 4:13). But a reader who imports the modern meaning everywhere will place half the Old Testament beside water that was never there.
webster_summary: A border, boundary, or territory — the side or edge of a region; only sometimes the seashore. The Authorized Version uses it chiefly in the older and wider sense.
webster_full: COAST, n. The exterior line, limit, or border of a country.
The edge or margin of the land next to the sea; the seashore.
From the Latin costa, a rib, a side; Old French coste.
In Scripture, usually the border or territory of a region (Exo 10:4; Mat 2:16).
Hence coasts in the plural: the parts or districts of a country.
scriptures: Exo 10:4
Else, if thou refuse to let my people go, behold, to morrow will I bring the locusts into thy coast:
And the LORD spake unto Moses and Aaron in mount Hor, by the coast of the land of Edom, saying,
Mat 2:16

Then Herod, when he saw that he was mocked of the wise men, was exceeding wroth, and sent forth, and slew all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had diligently enquired of the wise men.
Mat 4:13
And leaving Nazareth, he came and dwelt in Capernaum, which is upon the sea coast, in the borders of Zabulon and Nephthalim:
corruption_summary: Reading modern senses into old words quietly rewrites the text — and the wider habit, treating boundaries themselves as arbitrary, runs against a Bible in which God sets bounds to seas, nations, and fields.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The immediate hazard is lexical anachronism, the same error that trips readers on let, prevent, conversation, and wench. A reader who takes coast to mean shoreline will put Bethlehem on the sea and locusts on a beach, and will never know he has misread anything, because the sentence still makes a kind of sense. That is what makes the error stubborn: it does not announce itself. The remedy is the ordinary discipline of reading an old book with a dictionary of its own period, which is precisely what this dictionary exists to supply.

Recover the plain sense: the word means a border, and borders are a serious biblical category. God hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation; He shut up the sea with doors and said hitherto shalt thou come, but no further; He forbade removing the ancient landmark, and Job counts among the wicked those who remove the landmarks and violently take away flocks. A world in which every boundary is negotiable — of nations, of property, of office, of the created orders themselves — is not the world Scripture describes. The coasts were set by the One who appointed them, and the fact that He set them is what makes them worth respecting.
roots_summary: Latin costa, a side — a border or territory; in the AV rarely the seashore, and always a boundary God has set.
roots_lines: Coast — Latin costa, a rib or side; Old French coste.
Hebrew gebul, a border, boundary, or territory.
Exo 10:4: locusts into Egypt’s coast — its territory, not its shore.
Mat 2:16: the coasts of Bethlehem, some fifteen miles from any sea.
Mat 4:13 uses the shoreline sense: Capernaum upon the sea coast.
usage: Assume border before shore whenever the AV says coast.
Compare the same anachronism trap in let, prevent, and conversation.
Scripture treats boundaries as appointed: the sea, the nations, the landmark.

etymology: The Authorized Version’s form of defensed, from defence — Latin defendere, to ward off. A defenced city is a fortified city, walled and garrisoned; the word describes a place made strong against assault.
biblical_def: A defenced city is a fortified one, and Isaiah uses the word almost entirely to show such cities falling. “Thou hast made of a city an heap; of a defenced city a ruin: a palace of strangers to be no city; it shall never be built” (Isa 25:2). And again, “the defenced city shall be desolate, and the habitation forsaken, and left like a wilderness: there shall the calf feed” (Isa 27:10) — cattle grazing where walls stood. The historical instance is Sennacherib, who “came up against all the defenced cities of Judah, and took them” (Isa 36:1); every fortress in the kingdom fell, and only Jerusalem was left, and Jerusalem was delivered by an angel rather than by masonry. God then says something remarkable to the Assyrian himself: “Hast thou not heard long ago, how I have done it; and of ancient times, that I have formed it? now have I brought it to pass, that thou shouldest be to lay waste defenced cities into ruinous heaps” (Isa 37:26). The conqueror was an instrument, and did not know it. Yet the same word is used once in the opposite direction, and it is one of the great promises to a frightened minister: “I have made thee this day a defenced city, and an iron pillar, and brasen walls against the whole land” (Jer 1:18). Cities of stone fall; God fortifies men.
webster_summary: Fortified; walled and garrisoned against attack. Used in Isaiah chiefly of strong cities that nevertheless fell, and once of a prophet made strong by God.
webster_full: DEFENCED, pp. Fortified; guarded; secured against attack.
The older form of defensed; from defence, Latin defendere, to ward off.
Of a city: surrounded with walls and works of defence (Isa 36:1).
DEFENCE, n. That which guards or protects; fortification; resistance.
Jer 1:18 applies the term figuratively to a man made strong by God.
scriptures: Isa 25:2
For thou hast made of a city an heap; of a defenced city a ruin: a palace of strangers to be no city; it shall never be built.
Isa 36:1
Now it came to pass in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah, that Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the defenced cities of Judah, and took them.
Hast thou not heard long ago, how I have done it; and of ancient times, that I have formed it? now have I brought it to pass, that thou shouldest be to lay waste defenced cities into ruinous heaps.
Jer 1:18

For, behold, I have made thee this day a defenced city, and an iron pillar, and brasen walls against the whole land, against the kings of Judah, against the princes thereof, against the priests thereof, and against the people of the land.
corruption_summary: Security is sought in structures — walls, systems, reserves, institutions — and Isaiah’s repeated point is that the defenced city is precisely the thing that falls.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is misplaced confidence in structures. Every generation builds what it takes to be unassailable — walls, treaties, reserves, institutions, retirement accounts, reputations — and each generation is surprised when they fail. Isaiah writes as if the surprise itself were the folly. He has watched the strongest cities of Judah taken one after another by Assyria, and he draws the conclusion that fortification is not the same as safety. The point is not that walls are wrong; Nehemiah built them and God approved. The point is that a wall is a means, and a means trusted as an end becomes an idol that will certainly disappoint its worshippers.

Recover the plain sense: Isa 37:26 supplies the sovereignty that makes sense of the ruins. Sennacherib imagined he was making history and was told he was executing a purpose formed of ancient times — now have I brought it to pass. Nothing fell by accident. And the promise of Jer 1:18 supplies the comfort, for it moves the fortification from the stone to the man. Jeremiah was a young man told he would face kings, princes, priests, and the people of the land, and God did not promise him a quiet ministry; He promised they shall fight against thee; but they shall not prevail against thee. The city that survived Sennacherib survived by an angel, and the prophet who survived Judah survived because God made him a defenced city.
roots_summary: Latin defendere, to ward off — fortified; in Isaiah the cities that fell, and in Jeremiah the man God made strong.
roots_lines: Defenced — the AV form of defensed; Latin defendere, to ward off.
Of a city: walled, garrisoned, and provisioned against siege.
Isa 36:1: Sennacherib took all the defenced cities of Judah.
Isa 37:26: the conqueror was executing a purpose formed of ancient times.
Jer 1:18: God makes a man a defenced city, an iron pillar, and brasen walls.
usage: In Isaiah the defenced city is characteristically the thing that falls.
Walls are a lawful means; a means trusted as an end becomes an idol.
Jerusalem survived by an angel, not by masonry.

etymology: From the Latin magnificus, great in deed or appearance — magnus, great, and facere, to make. An older English form of magnificent, signifying grand and splendid, built on a great scale.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, and it is David’s reason for the greatest building project in Israel’s history: “Solomon my son is young and tender, and the house that is to be builded for the LORD must be exceeding magnifical, of fame and of glory throughout all countries: I will therefore now make preparation for it” (1Ch 22:5). Three things are packed into that sentence. First, David judges the house should be splendid, not because God dwells in temples made with hands — David knew better, and said so — but because the building was to testify throughout all countries; its magnificence was missionary. Second, he acknowledges his son’s inexperience: young and tender. And third, he draws the practical conclusion that a father draws — I will therefore now make preparation for it. David gathered iron, brass beyond weighing, cedar without number, and workmen, for a house he had been expressly forbidden to build and would never see. He had asked to build it and been told no, because he had shed blood abundantly; and having been refused, he spent the rest of his life preparing materials for the man who would. That is a rare grace. Most men who are told the work is not theirs either abandon it or resent whoever gets it.
webster_summary: Grand, splendid, built on a great scale; an older form of magnificent, used of the house David prepared for Solomon to build.
webster_full: MAGNIFICAL, adj. Grand; splendid; illustrious; magnificent.
From the Latin magnificus, from magnus, great, and facere, to make.
An older form, now superseded by magnificent.
Applied to buildings, works, and undertakings of great scale and splendour.
1Ch 22:5 is the sole occurrence in the Authorized Version.
scriptures: And David said, Solomon my son is young and tender, and the house that is to be builded for the LORD must be exceeding magnifical, of fame and of glory throughout all countries: I will therefore now make preparation for it. So David prepared abundantly before his death.
And David said to Solomon, My son, as for me, it was in my mind to build an house unto the name of the LORD my God:

But the word of the LORD came to me, saying, Thou hast shed blood abundantly, and hast made great wars: thou shalt not build an house unto my name, because thou hast shed much blood upon the earth in my sight.

Furthermore David the king said unto all the congregation, Solomon my son, whom alone God hath chosen, is yet young and tender, and the work is great: for the palace is not for man, but for the LORD God.
corruption_summary: Ministry is measured by what a man completes in his own lifetime, so the work of preparing for a successor one will never see looks like failure rather than the faithfulness David showed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live temptation the passage exposes is the demand to see one’s own work finished. Modern ministry, business, and even parenting are measured in completed projects attributable to a named individual within a career, and a man who spends his best years amassing materials for someone else’s building will be counted to have achieved nothing. David is the standing rebuke. He wanted to build the house; he was refused, and told plainly why — thou hast shed blood abundantly, and hast made great wars (1Ch 22:8). He accepted the refusal, and then did the one thing that neither resentment nor resignation would have done: he prepared.

Recover the plain sense: God’s work spans generations, and no servant sees the whole of it. Moses brought Israel to Jordan and died on Nebo; the patriarchs died in faith not having received the promises; the prophets ministered things reported to us and not to themselves; and the temple David planned was built by a son whose reign he did not live to see. To labour for a harvest another man reaps is not the exception in Scripture but very nearly the rule — one soweth, and another reapeth. The question is not whether you will finish, which you will not, but whether what you leave will be ready to be built on. David left iron, brass, cedar, and a charge. That is what a father leaves.
roots_summary: Latin magnificus, made great — splendid; David’s word for the house he prepared and never built.
roots_lines: Magnifical — Latin magnus + facere, to make great.
An older form of magnificent, now obsolete.
1Ch 22:5 is its only occurrence in the Authorized Version.
The splendour was missionary: of fame and of glory throughout all countries.
1Ch 22:8: David was refused the building because he had shed blood abundantly.
usage: David prepared materials for a house he was forbidden to build and would never see.
The magnificence was aimed outward — a testimony throughout all countries.
Scripture’s norm is that one sows and another reaps.

etymology: From the Old French patron, a model or exemplar, and that from the Latin patronus, a protector or original — the same word as patron, the two senses having separated in English. A pattern is the original from which copies are made.
biblical_def: A pattern is an original shown, from which a copy is to be made, and the doctrine attached to it is large. Moses is told, “According to all that I shew thee, after the pattern of the tabernacle, and the pattern of all the instruments thereof, even so shall ye make it” (Exo 25:9), and again, “look that thou make them after their pattern, which was shewed thee in the mount” (Exo 25:40). The margin renders the phrase which thou wast caused to see. Moses did not design the tabernacle; he copied it, and even the candlestick was made “according unto the pattern which the LORD had shewed Moses” (Num 8:4). Hebrews draws the conclusion the Old Testament had been preparing: the priests “serve unto the example and shadow of heavenly things, as Moses was admonished of God” (Heb 8:5) — the tabernacle in the wilderness was a copy of something real, and the reality is in heaven. That is why the details mattered so exactly; a copyist has no liberty to improve his original. The word takes one further turn in Paul’s hands, where a man becomes the pattern: “for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first Jesus Christ might shew forth all longsuffering, for a pattern to them which should hereafter believe” (1Ti 1:16). The chief of sinners is exhibited as the specimen case of mercy.
webster_summary: An original or model from which a copy is made; in Exodus the heavenly original shewed to Moses, and in Paul a man exhibited as the specimen of mercy.
webster_full: PATTERN, n. An original or model proposed for imitation; an exemplar.
A specimen; a part shewn as a sample of the whole.
From the Old French patron, a model; Latin patronus, a protector, an original.
In the arts, the form from which a mould or copy is taken.
Exo 25:40: after their pattern, which was shewed thee in the mount.
scriptures: Exo 25:9
According to all that I shew thee, after the pattern of the tabernacle, and the pattern of all the instruments thereof, even so shall ye make it.
And look that thou make them after their pattern, which was shewed thee in the mount.
Heb 8:5

Who serve unto the example and shadow of heavenly things, as Moses was admonished of God when he was about to make the tabernacle: for, See, saith he, that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount.
Howbeit for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first Jesus Christ might shew forth all longsuffering, for a pattern to them which should hereafter believe on him to life everlasting.
corruption_summary: Worship and church order are treated as matters of design open to innovation, where the tabernacle pattern establishes that God shews the original and man copies it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the copyist claiming an author’s liberty. Modern church practice largely assumes that the forms of worship and the shape of church life are ours to design, subject only to taste, culture, and effectiveness; and any appeal to a fixed pattern is heard as legalism. Exodus assumes the opposite. Moses is shewn a pattern in the mount and told six separate times in the following chapters to make things as it was shewed thee, down to the loops, the taches, the weights of gold, and the colours of the yarn. The reason is given in Hebrews: these things were copies of heavenly realities. To alter the copy is to misrepresent the original, which is not creativity but falsification.

Recover the plain sense: this is the ground of the reformed principle that God regulates His own worship, and it is not a cramping doctrine but a liberating one. A servant who must invent is under infinite pressure; a servant who must copy has only to look at what he was shewn. Note also that the pattern is always shewn before it is required — God does not command a copy without providing an original. And take the turn Paul gives the word as the gospel’s own use of it. He calls himself a pattern of mercy: if longsuffering could reach a blasphemer and a persecutor, the specimen has been established, and no later sinner can plead that his case is beyond the sample.
roots_summary: Old French patron, a model — the original from which copies are made; shewn to Moses in the mount, and shewn in Paul as mercy’s specimen.
roots_lines: Pattern — Old French patron, a model; Latin patronus, an original.
The same word as patron; the senses parted in English.
Exo 25:40 margin: which thou wast caused to see.
Heb 8:5: the tabernacle was the example and shadow of heavenly things.
1Ti 1:16: Paul himself a pattern to them which should hereafter believe.
usage: A copyist has no liberty to improve his original — hence the exactness of Exodus.
God always shews the pattern before requiring the copy.
Paul as pattern: if mercy reached the chief of sinners, the sample is established.

etymology: From bishop (Greek episkopos, an overseer) and the Saxon ric, dominion, rule, or jurisdiction — the same element as in bishopric and the German Reich. The office and charge of an overseer.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, and it settles a matter of church order: “For it is written in the book of Psalms, Let his habitation be desolate, and let no man dwell therein: and his bishoprick let another take” (Act 1:20). Peter is speaking of Judas, and the striking thing is what he calls the vacancy. The traitor’s place among the twelve is an office — the Greek is episkope, an overseership — and it is a thing that can be vacated and filled. Peter reasons from two psalms, sets the qualification (a man who companied with them all the time the Lord Jesus went in and out among them, and a witness of the resurrection), the company puts forward two, they pray, and “the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles” (Act 1:26). Several doctrines stand together in that short account. The church has offices, not merely gifted individuals; offices have qualifications, which are stated and not assumed; the congregation is involved in the choosing; and the outcome is committed to God. Paul later takes up the same word without embarrassment: “If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work” (1Ti 3:1) — and then gives a list of qualifications that is almost entirely about character rather than ability.
webster_summary: The office, charge, and jurisdiction of a bishop or overseer; in Acts, the vacated office of Judas which another was appointed to take.
webster_full: BISHOPRICK, n. A diocese; the district over which the jurisdiction of a bishop extends.
The charge or office of a bishop or overseer.
From bishop, Greek episkopos, an overseer, and the Saxon ric, jurisdiction or rule.
Rendering the Greek episkope, oversight, the office of an overseer (Act 1:20).
1Ti 3:1 renders the same word the office of a bishop.
scriptures: Act 1:20
For it is written in the book of Psalms, Let his habitation be desolate, and let no man dwell therein : and his bishoprick let another take.
Act 1:26
And they gave forth their lots; and the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.
This is a true saying, If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
corruption_summary: Church leadership is drifting toward personality and platform, where Scripture speaks of an office with stated qualifications that a congregation recognises and a man may be removed from.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the replacement of office by personality. Increasingly a man leads because of what he can gather — his following, his platform, his communicative gift — rather than because he has been examined against a standard and set apart by a congregation. The consequences are visible: no clear qualification to test him by before he rises, and no clear mechanism to remove him when he falls, since one cannot vacate an office one never formally held. Act 1 assumes the opposite at every point. Judas had an episkope; it was a definable thing; it could be forfeited; and it had to be filled by a man meeting stated conditions.

Recover the plain sense: the biblical order protects both flock and pastor. It protects the flock, because a man is examined by a standard the congregation can read — and 1Ti 3 sets that standard overwhelmingly in terms of character rather than gift: blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, given to hospitality, not greedy of filthy lucre, one that ruleth well his own house. It protects the pastor, because a man who holds an office serves under a description rather than under the impossible burden of being perpetually impressive. And Act 20:28 names the ground of the whole thing: the overseers are to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood. Whatever the office is worth, it is worth that.
roots_summary: Greek episkope, oversight, with Saxon ric, jurisdiction — the office of an overseer; Judas’s place, vacated and filled.
roots_lines: Bishoprick — bishop (Greek episkopos, overseer) + Saxon ric, rule.
The same element ric stands in the German Reich.
Renders the Greek episkope, oversight or the office of oversight.
Act 1:20: Judas’s place is treated as an office that another may take.
1Ti 3:1 renders the identical word the office of a bishop.
usage: Act 1 shows an office with stated qualifications, congregational involvement, and prayer.
1Ti 3’s qualifications are almost entirely of character, not ability.
Act 20:28 grounds the office in the blood by which the church was purchased.

etymology: From the Latin cogitare, to think or ponder — co, together, and agitare, to turn over. Cogitations are thoughts turned over repeatedly in the mind, deliberate and revolving rather than passing.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, at the close of Daniel’s vision of the four beasts: “Hitherto is the end of the matter. As for me Daniel, my cogitations much troubled me, and my countenance changed in me: but I kept the matter in my heart” (Dan 7:28). Three things are recorded, and each is worth notice. His thoughts much troubled him — the prophet who received the revelation was disturbed by it, which should quiet anyone who imagines that receiving truth from God is a comfortable business. His countenance changed: the trouble was not private but showed in his face, as it did in Belshazzar’s and in Nehemiah’s. And then, “I kept the matter in my heart” — he did not publish his disturbance, discharge it on the nearest listener, or make his own agitation the subject. The etymology is exactly right for what Daniel describes: cogitare is to turn a thing over, and these were thoughts revolving without resolution. Note that Daniel is not rebuked for them. Scripture nowhere requires that the believer feel settled about everything God has shown him. Mary kept all these things and pondered them in her heart; the psalmists ask how long without answer; and Daniel goes on serving under three kings with an unresolved vision turning in his mind.
webster_summary: Deep and revolving thoughts; meditations turned over repeatedly in the mind, as Daniel’s after his vision.
webster_full: COGITATION, n. The act of thinking; thought; meditation; contemplation.
From the Latin cogitare, to think, from co and agitare, to agitate or turn over.
In the plural, the successive or revolving thoughts of the mind.
Purpose or design formed in the mind.
Dan 7:28 is the sole occurrence in the Authorized Version.
scriptures: Dan 7:28
Hitherto is the end of the matter. As for me Daniel, my cogitations much troubled me, and my countenance changed in me: but I kept the matter in my heart.
Dan 7:15
I Daniel was grieved in my spirit in the midst of my body, and the visions of my head troubled me.
Luk 2:19
But Mary kept all these things , and pondered them in her heart.
Psa 77:6
I call to remembrance my song in the night: I commune with mine own heart: and my spirit made diligent search.
corruption_summary: Unsettled thoughts are now treated as a condition to be resolved or medicated away, so a believer troubled by what God has shown him concludes something is wrong with his faith.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live distortion is the expectation of settledness. Contemporary religious culture prizes the testimony that resolves, the answer that satisfies, the peace that arrives on schedule; and a Christian whose thoughts keep turning without conclusion is likely to be told he lacks faith, or to conclude it himself. Daniel makes that verdict impossible. He was a man of extraordinary faith — the lions’ den is in the next chapter — and his cogitations much troubled him, visibly, and the book does not say they stopped. What God had shown him about the beasts and the little horn was genuinely disturbing, and being disturbed by disturbing truth is not a failure of grace but a mark of paying attention.

Recover the plain sense: there is a right way to hold an unresolved trouble, and Daniel models it. He kept the matter in his heart — neither denying it nor broadcasting it, neither pretending to a peace he had not been given nor making his agitation everyone else’s business. Mary did the same with things she could not yet understand. Asaph in Psa 77 says his spirit made diligent search and the answer did not come until he remembered the works of the LORD of old. That is the pattern: keep the matter, keep serving, and keep bringing it back to what God has already done. Daniel served under three kings with an unfinished vision turning in his mind, and the vision was true all the while he could not settle it.
roots_summary: Latin cogitare, to turn over — revolving thoughts; Daniel’s trouble after the vision, kept in his heart.
roots_lines: Cogitations — Latin cogitare, from co + agitare, to turn over.
The etymology implies revolving, not passing, thought.
Dan 7:28 is the only occurrence in the Authorized Version.
Dan 7:15 says his spirit was grieved in the midst of his body.
Compare Luk 2:19, where Mary kept and pondered what she could not yet understand.
usage: The prophet who received the revelation was disturbed by it.
The trouble showed in his countenance and was still kept in his heart.
Being troubled by disturbing truth is attention, not weak faith.

etymology: From the Old French devis, a division or arrangement, and that from the Latin dividere, to divide — hence a thing devised, a plan, contrivance, or scheme. A device is thought worked into a design.
biblical_def: A device in Scripture is a contrivance of the mind, and the word is used of three schemers. Men devise: “There are many devices in a man’s heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand” (Pro 19:21) — the two halves of that verse hold the whole doctrine of providence, human plans genuinely made and a divine counsel that is not thereby put at risk. The wicked devise in particular: “The wicked in his pride doth persecute the poor: let them be taken in the devices that they have imagined” (Psa 10:2), a prayer that the trap should catch the trapper, which is the regular shape of biblical justice — Haman on his own gallows. Satan devises: “Lest Satan should get an advantage of us: for we are not ignorant of his devices” (2Co 2:11) — and the context of that famous sentence is worth recovering, for Paul is not warning about the occult or gross temptation but about a church failing to forgive a repentant offender. That is the devil’s device in view: a congregation so severe with a restored sinner that he is swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. And God overrules all devising: “He disappointeth the devices of the crafty, so that their hands cannot perform their enterprise” (Job 5:12). Three devisers, and only one counsel that stands.
webster_summary: Contrivances, schemes, or plans formed in the mind; used of the plans of men, the plots of the wicked, and the stratagems of Satan.
webster_full: DEVICE, n. That which is formed by design; a contrivance; an invention.
A scheme formed; a project; stratagem; artifice; often in an ill sense.
An emblem or figure designed to represent a family or a purpose.
From the Old French devis; Latin dividere, to divide, to distribute.
2Co 2:11: we are not ignorant of his devices — the stratagems of Satan.
scriptures: Job 5:12
He disappointeth the devices of the crafty, so that their hands cannot perform their enterprise.
Psa 10:2
The wicked in his pride doth persecute the poor: let them be taken in the devices that they have imagined.
There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand.
Lest Satan should get an advantage of us: for we are not ignorant of his devices.
corruption_summary: 2Co 2:11 is quoted almost exclusively in warnings about the occult or gross temptation, when Paul’s stated context is a church refusing to restore a repentant man.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the misdirection of a famous verse. We are not ignorant of his devices has become the standard epigraph for teaching on spiritual warfare in its dramatic forms — the occult, the demonic, the sensational temptation — and while Satan certainly works in those ways, that is not what Paul is discussing. Read the preceding verses. A man had been disciplined by the Corinthian church; the punishment inflicted of many was sufficient; and Paul urges them to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. Then: lest Satan get an advantage of us, for we are not ignorant of his devices. The device is unforgiveness in a congregation that was right to discipline and is now wrong to withhold restoration.

Recover the plain sense: the adversary works most successfully through churches doing something legitimate slightly too long. Discipline is commanded; discipline that will not end when repentance comes is a trap, and Paul says plainly whose trap it is. That is a searching thought for congregations proud of their seriousness. Set it beside Pro 19:21 for the comfort that governs the whole subject: men devise and the devil devises, and the counsel of the LORD shall stand. Job 5:12 completes it — God disappoints the devices of the crafty so that their hands cannot perform their enterprise. The schemes are real; not one of them is sovereign.
roots_summary: Latin dividere, to divide — a thing devised; the plans of men, the plots of the wicked, the stratagems of Satan.
roots_lines: Devices — Old French devis, from Latin dividere, to divide or arrange.
A device is thought worked into a design or contrivance.
Pro 19:21: many devices in a man’s heart; the counsel of the LORD shall stand.
Psa 10:2 prays that the schemers be taken in their own devices.
2Co 2:11: the device in view is a church refusing to restore the repentant.
usage: Read 2Co 2:11 with 2Co 2:7 — the device is unforgiveness after discipline.
Psa 10:2 asks that the trap take the trapper; compare Haman’s gallows.
Job 5:12: God disappoints devices so that hands cannot perform the enterprise.

etymology: From the Latin superfluus, overflowing — super, above, and fluere, to flow. That which flows over the top; excess, overplus, more than is needed or contained.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, in James’s instruction on receiving the word: “Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls” (Jas 1:21). The image is agricultural and surgical at once. Superfluity of naughtiness is the overflow of wickedness — evil so abundant that it runs over the sides — and the verb lay apart is the word for stripping off a garment. James is describing a man taking off filthy clothes before receiving something into himself. Then comes the striking word engrafted: the word of God is to be received as a graft is received into a stock, which requires a cut, an insertion, and a binding, and which results in the graft’s nature prevailing over the stock’s. Note the order James insists on. Stripping comes before receiving, and meekness is the manner of receiving — not because the stripping earns the word, but because a man cannot receive a graft while refusing the knife. And observe what the engrafted word is said to do: it is able to save your souls. James, so often accused of preaching mere morality, here makes the word of God the instrument of salvation and meekness the posture of the saved.
webster_summary: Overflow or excess; more than enough. In Jas 1:21, the overflowing abundance of wickedness that must be stripped off before the word is received.
webster_full: SUPERFLUITY, n. A greater quantity than is wanted; superabundance.
That which is beyond what is necessary or useful.
From the Latin superfluus, from super, above, and fluere, to flow.
Jas 1:21: superfluity of naughtiness, the overflow of wickedness.
Naughtiness in the older English is wickedness, not mere mischief.
scriptures: Jas 1:21
Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls.
Jas 1:22
But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
Wherefore laying aside all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all evil speakings,
As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby :
corruption_summary: Naughtiness has softened into a word for childish mischief, so a verse about the overflow of wickedness now sounds like a caution against harmless naughty behaviour.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The distortion is the softening of naughtiness. In 1611 the word meant wickedness outright — a naughty person was a worthless and evil one, as when Jeremiah’s bad figs are called naughty figs, or Eliab accuses David of a naughty heart. Modern English has reduced it to the mild misbehaviour of children, so that superfluity of naughtiness now sounds almost playful. The result is that one of the sharpest commands in the epistles reads like a caution against being a bit cheeky. Restore the word and the sentence recovers its edge: strip off, as a filthy garment, the overflowing abundance of your wickedness.

Recover the plain sense: James is not describing a tidy-up but a stripping, and the reason is the graft. A word received as an engrafted thing is not information added to a man but a nature introduced into him, and grafting requires a wound. Peter uses the identical structure: laying aside all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all evil speakings, as newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word (1Pe 2:1–2). Put off, then take in. And James will not let the receiving stay theoretical, for the very next verse says be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. The graft that takes will bear its own fruit, and a graft that bears nothing was never joined.
roots_summary: Latin super + fluere, to flow over — excess; the overflow of wickedness stripped off before the word is engrafted.
roots_lines: Superfluity — Latin superfluus, overflowing.
Jas 1:21 is its only occurrence in the Authorized Version.
Naughtiness in older English means wickedness (Jer 24:2; 1Sa 17:28).
Lay apart renders a verb for stripping off a garment.
Engrafted implies a cut, an insertion, and a nature that prevails.
usage: Read naughtiness as wickedness, not childish mischief.
The order is stripping, then receiving, then doing (Jas 1:21–22).
1Pe 2:1–2 uses the identical put-off-then-take-in structure.

etymology: From the Latin terrestris, belonging to the earth, from terra, the earth. Of or pertaining to the earth, as celestial is of the heavens; the two words are set in deliberate contrast by Paul.
biblical_def: The word belongs to Paul’s great argument on the resurrection body: “There are also celestial bodies, and bodies terrestrial: but the glory of the celestial is one, and the glory of the terrestrial is another” (1Co 15:40). He is answering the scoffing question with what body do they come? and his method is to multiply examples of God’s power to give differing bodies. There is more than one kind of flesh; there are bodies of earth and bodies of sky; and even within the sky, “there is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars: for one star differeth from another star in glory” (1Co 15:41). The point is not that the resurrection body is a star but that God’s repertoire of bodies is vast, and the objector’s failure of imagination is no argument. Then comes the conclusion: “It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body” (1Co 15:44). Note that spiritual there does not mean immaterial — the risen Christ ate broiled fish and invited Thomas to handle Him. It means a body animated and governed by the Spirit rather than by the mere soul-life of Adam. The Christian hope is not escape from a body but the raising of one, and the terrestrial is not despised. It is sown.
webster_summary: Belonging to the earth; earthly, as distinguished from celestial, belonging to the heavens. Used by Paul in his argument for the resurrection body.
webster_full: TERRESTRIAL, adj. Pertaining to the earth; existing on the earth; earthly.
From the Latin terrestris, from terra, the earth.
Consisting of earth; as, terrestrial matter.
Opposed to celestial, which pertains to the heavens.
1Co 15:40 sets the two in contrast to illustrate differing glories of bodies.
scriptures: There are also celestial bodies, and bodies terrestrial: but the glory of the celestial is one, and the glory of the terrestrial is another.
There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars: for one star differeth from another star in glory.
It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body.
For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.
corruption_summary: The Christian hope is popularly imagined as disembodied souls in a spiritual realm — a Greek idea, not a biblical one — where Paul’s whole argument is for a body raised.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is Platonism wearing Christian clothes. The picture most people carry — including a great many believers — is of the soul escaping the body at death and existing thereafter in a bodiless spiritual state, with matter left behind as the discarded husk of a lower existence. That is Greek philosophy, not Scripture. The Bible’s hope is resurrection: the same person raised, embodied, glorified. The confusion is helped along by the word spiritual in 1Co 15:44, which readers take to mean non-physical. Paul means a body enlivened and ruled by the Spirit, in contrast to the natural or soulish body of the first Adam. He is contrasting two animating principles, not matter with non-matter.

Recover the plain sense: the risen Christ is the specimen, and He was unmistakably physical — He showed His hands and His feet, said a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have, ate before them, and bore the marks. He is the firstfruits, which means His body is the pattern of ours. And note what this implies for the present: the body is not a temporary container for the real self but part of what is redeemed, which is why Scripture legislates for it, why fornication is a sin against one’s own body, and why burial rather than disposal has been the Christian instinct. This corruptible must put on incorruption (1Co 15:53) — this one. Not a replacement, and not an escape.
roots_summary: Latin terra, the earth — earthly, set against celestial; Paul’s illustration of the many glories God can give a body.
roots_lines: Terrestrial — Latin terrestris, from terra, the earth.
Set in deliberate contrast with celestial, of the heavens.
1Co 15:40–41 multiplies examples: earth, sky, sun, moon, star differing from star.
1Co 15:44: spiritual body means Spirit-animated, not immaterial.
1Co 15:53: this corruptible must put on incorruption.
usage: Paul’s answer to with what body do they come? is the variety of bodies God already makes.
Spiritual contrasts animating principles, not matter with non-matter.
The risen Christ ate and was handled — He is the pattern of the raised body.

etymology: The Authorized Version’s spelling of recompense, from the Latin recompensare — re, back, and compensare, to weigh together. A recompence is a weighing-back: requital rendered in exact proportion, whether of reward or of punishment.
biblical_def: Recompence is requital weighed out, and Scripture assigns it emphatically to God. “To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence; their foot shall slide in due time” (Deu 32:35) — a verse Paul quotes to forbid private revenge: “avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” (Rom 12:19). The logic is not that vengeance is wrong in itself but that it belongs to Someone, and taking it is theft as much as sin. The same word then does duty in the gospel. To the fearful Isaiah says, “Be strong, fear not: behold, your God will come with vengeance, even God with a recompence; he will come and save you” (Isa 35:4). Notice how that verse is built: the recompence and the salvation are the same coming. God’s settling of accounts is the deliverance of the oppressed, which is why the poor and the persecuted in Scripture pray for judgment rather than dreading it. Solomon states the principle in ordinary life — “the recompence of a man’s hands shall be rendered unto him” (Pro 12:14) — and Job warns that for the deceived, “vanity shall be his recompence” (Job 15:31), a man paid back in the very currency he chose.
webster_summary: Requital weighed back in proportion — reward or punishment. In Scripture, chiefly God’s prerogative, and the reason private revenge is forbidden.
webster_full: RECOMPENCE, RECOMPENSE, n. An equivalent returned for anything given, done, or suffered.
Compensation; reward; amends for injury or loss.
Requital; retribution; punishment weighed to the offence.
From the Latin re and compensare, to weigh together, to counterbalance.
Deu 32:35: To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence.
scriptures: To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence; their foot shall slide in due time: for the day of their calamity is at hand, and the things that shall come upon them make haste.
A man shall be satisfied with good by the fruit of his mouth: and the recompence of a man's hands shall be rendered unto him.
Isa 35:4
Say to them that are of a fearful heart, Be strong, fear not: behold, your God will come with vengeance, even God with a recompence; he will come and save you.
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
corruption_summary: Divine retribution is dismissed as unworthy of a loving God, which removes the only ground Scripture gives the wronged for laying down their own vengeance.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the sentimental rejection of retribution. It is widely held that a God of love cannot also be a God who repays, and that the language of vengeance belongs to a primitive stratum of religion the church should outgrow. The dictionary rejects this. It is not merely that Scripture teaches divine recompence from Deuteronomy to Revelation; it is that removing it makes the New Testament’s ethics impossible. Paul’s command not to avenge oneself rests entirely on the promise that God will: avenge not yourselves, for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay. Take away the second clause and the first is not mercy but a demand that the wronged accept permanent injustice.

Recover the plain sense: the doctrine of recompence is what makes forgiveness possible for people who have suffered real wrongs. A man can release his grip on a debt precisely because he knows the books will be balanced by One who sees what he cannot and judges without error. He is not asked to pretend the wrong did not happen or that it does not matter; he is asked to hand it to the proper court. And Isa 35:4 shows the same truth in its gospel dress: the coming that brings recompence is the coming that saves, so that for those who trust Him the settling of accounts is not a terror but a rescue. The oppressed in Scripture do not fear the judgment. They pray, How long, O Lord?
roots_summary: Latin re + compensare, to weigh back — exact requital; God’s prerogative, and the ground on which revenge is forbidden.
roots_lines: Recompence — the AV spelling; Latin recompensare, to weigh back.
The image is a balance: requital weighed to the offence or the service.
Deu 32:35, quoted at Rom 12:19 to forbid private revenge.
Pro 12:14: the recompence of a man’s hands shall be rendered unto him.
Isa 35:4 joins recompence and salvation in one coming.
usage: Revenge is forbidden because it belongs to God, not because requital is wrong.
Isa 35:4: the coming with recompence is the coming that saves.
The doctrine is what makes forgiveness possible for the genuinely wronged.
